post.title: Conversations With Cade Metz on the Rationalists

contents.markdown:
This was interesting! It is funny to see the few moments when Cade Metz *deflects understanding*.

Most obviously the part about Scott Alexander. Hey, I only *threatened* to ruin his life by exposing his identity, but I *didn't actually do it* (because he prevented me from doing so), so why is everyone treating me like the bad guy?

By the same logic, if I shoot at someone but miss them, hey, I didn't *do* them any harm; no hard feelings, right?

More subtle is the part about the Sequences. He wants to know what they are about, but he wants it in a different sense than you try to explain. He is not looking for substance, only for buzzwords. He wants to be able to describe the Sequences to his audience, without getting into the technical details; he wants to stay impartial, even to the degree that if the Sequences said "2+2=4", he wants to merely report it as "some people believe that..." without providing any judgement about whether the equation is correct or not.

As an analogy, imagine that you are writing about a religious cult, let's say one that worships Krishna. You want to know what their beliefs are about, in the sense that you want the right passwords, such as "reincarnation". But if the guy who is explaining their beliefs to you says, "dude, I don't think you really grok how Lord Krishna *is* the cosmic consciousness, let me show you the specific verse of the Gita again", you will be like "no thank you, I already know all that I wanted to know". You wanted to know *about* the holy books, not to be converted by them.

Similarly, Cade Metz wants to know *about* the rationalist "holy texts", not to be converted by them. Even if the texts contained things like "2+2=4", he wants to remain impartial. Admitting that 2+2 actually equals 4 would be failing as a journalist. He wants to report the buzzwords that the cultists hiding in the walled compound worship.

> Tell me about the comment section at *Overcoming Bias*. \[...\] Did everybody use their real names? \[...\] How do you view the real name versus not real name? It's a big part of the community. \[...\] Why are people so concerned with using a pseudonym? \[...\] Do you think that the adherence to that is stronger in your community than in others?

He seems fishing for something. The idea that "some people use real names, some people use pseudonyms, it's everyone's own business, duh" is clearly *not* what what he wanted to hear.

My guess (just a guess) was that he was looking either for "Scott Alexander is weird even from the perspective of our group, most rationalists use their real names openly" (which means that his insistence on using the real name was no big deal, even most rationalists are okay with that, it's only Scott making a mountain out of a mole hill), or "using real names is a taboo among rationalists" (cool fact about a cult, but also means that a non-member he is not bound by the social norms of the cultists).

> Isn't \[defer to rationalist leaders\] what's going on with this thing between Scott Alexander and me?

Oh my. He seems 100% incapable of admitting the possibility of doing something wrong. If people are angry about him trying to dox their favorite blogger, it must be because *all those people are wrong*. Now we finally know the truth -- Scott is wrong because whatever, and everyone else is wrong *because they defer to Scott*.

> You call them the internet weirdos, we can call it something nicer like the rationalist, the rationalist-slash-EA community or whatever you want to call it, it is this giant force in that world that in some ways has more power than the companies. \[...\] It's a different power, but it's power, and nobody knows about it. What I'm doing is explaining this to people, and showing how this happened. Where did this community come from, how did these ideas evolve.

I suspect this is going to become *The Protocols of the Elders of TESCREAL*.

Towards the end I get a feeling that I am listening to a frog negotiating with a scorpion and trying to extract a promise that he really really really won't sting it this time, and the scorpion doesn't even pretend too hard, he's just like "haha, don't worry, I will just do whatever feels natural to me at the moment, trust me bro". :(

> \[Ben Hoffman writes to Cade Metz: \] I wonder whether this confusing combination of curiosity and inhibition might have something to do with your understanding of journalistic ethics, which as far as I can tell you follow fastidiously. Specifically, I wonder whether something about the idea that it would be wrong to *get involved with* a story you're writing about, also makes it hard to take the sorts of actions that would lead to *understanding* the story.

Hah, that's what I wrote about. Nice to have it confirmed I am not the only one who gets this feeling.

I think that how Cade excuses it to himself, is that he is writing for plebs, and plebs don't care about facts, they only want to read celebrity trivia: who is friends with whom, who met whom on which day, etc. So he is translating the story for them, in their preferred format. They are "interested in ideas" but only on the level of buzzwords. (Just like relativity is "time flies fast when you are having fun" and quantum physics is "the cat is simultaneously dead and alive", rationality is "we live in a simulation and/or a Terminator movie".) So he is going to write a *human story* about how a smart guy joined a cult and started to believe that he was living in a simulation and defending humanity against an attack of sci-fi robots... but then he disagreed with the leader about some trans issues, started thinking critically, and gradually realized that the entire thing was a sham.

...omg, Cade starts again: "Why is every accusing me of doxing Scott? I only threatened credibly to do so. If he changed his life completely so that he does not need anonymity anymore, that couldn't possibly be my fault, right? People only say I am bad guy because they are a cultish hive mind." And Zack, heroically, repeats the same explanation for the 99-th time.

And then again. I admire you patience.

.

Some of these texts are old, so I am not sure -- is the book already out, or not?

If not, I think this would be a great opportunity, Zack, to make predictions about what will be in the book. Like, if you will read the book, you will probably say "good" to some parts, and "omg wtf" to others. Could you try to predict which will be which in advance? And then, evaluate your predictions?
To talk to a journalist is defection.

20 bucks says that the surreality quote ends up in the book lol. The transcript makes it sound like he perked up immediately there; he seemed waaaay more interested in that than your attempts to explain epistemology.

> So, if it isn't obvious, I am truly interested in what you are dealing with. You are already an important character in my book, and I think you can be even more important.

At first I felt it was insulting that Cade Metz thought this transparent ego-stroking would work. Then I realized you gave him the info he wanted anyway. Maybe it was level-2 bait: maybe he thought you'd be motivated to share more info in order to disclaim importance. See related thoughts by another [here.](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/MNRZL69FWkjNABd3T/conversation-among-cade-metz-michael-vassar-jessica-taylor?commentId=qChAvs5bKfxrDRksN)

But really, it works as level-1 bait too; as we all know, understanding that you're being flattered doesn't entirely prevent flattery from working.

But *really*, I guess you were going to give him the info he asked for just because he asked, so whatever galaxy-brain thing might have been going on, it was probably a waste... no, well, he did learn something about your self-view perhaps.

Dunno where I'm going with this but I found the interaction interesting.
